title: The Grandparent Phone Scam: Red Flags and How to Protect Family
bigPicture: Scammers pretend to be a family member in trouble and press you to send money fast. Slow down, hang up, and check with the real person at a number you already know.
whatYouNeedToKnow: The caller claims to be a family member or close friend who needs money. They may also pose as a lawyer, police officer, or doctor.
Scammers may know details from social media or a hacked email, or they may simply guess.
Some use AI to clone a loved one's voice from a short audio clip, so a familiar voice is not proof.
Red flags: demands for immediate payment, claims the situation is urgent and only you can help, requests to keep it secret, and pressure to act without checking.
Requests to pay by wire transfer (such as Western Union or MoneyGram), cryptocurrency, payment apps, or gift cards are a red flag.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Sending money before you check the story with your family member.
Keeping it secret because the caller told you to.
Letting emotion and urgency push you into acting without checking.
actionSteps: Resist the pressure. Hang up, or tell the caller you will call back.
If hanging up feels hard, ask a question only the real person would know.
Call or message your family member or friend at a number you already know is correct.
Contact another family member or friend, even if you were told to keep it secret.
If you already sent money, act as fast as you can. The FTC has general guidance on getting your money back.
Report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to your state attorney general.
